claim: The ellipsoid body (EB) in the Drosophila brain is a central complex (CX) substructure that harbors circumferentially laminated ring (R) neuron axons.
source: The ellipsoid body (EB) in the Drosophila brain is a central complex (CX) substructure that harbors circumferentially laminated ring (R) neuron axons and mediates multifaceted sensory integration and motor coordination functions.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the anatomical structure of the EB.

claim: The EB mediates multifaceted sensory integration and motor coordination functions.
source: The ellipsoid body (EB) in the Drosophila brain is a central complex (CX) substructure that harbors circumferentially laminated ring (R) neuron axons and mediates multifaceted sensory integration and motor coordination functions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the EB.

claim: The EB is sequentially innervated by small-field and large-field neurons.
source: We show here that the EB is sequentially innervated by small-field and large-field neurons and that early developing EB neurons play an important regulatory role in EB laminae formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by developmental imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Early developing EB neurons play an important regulatory role in EB laminae formation.
source: We show here that the EB is sequentially innervated by small-field and large-field neurons and that early developing EB neurons play an important regulatory role in EB laminae formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by ablation experiments in Figure 2.

claim: The transmembrane proteins semaphorin-1a (Sema-1a) and plexin A function together to regulate R axon lamination.
source: The transmembrane proteins semaphorin-1a (Sema-1a) and plexin A function together to regulate R axon lamination.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNAi and MARCM experiments in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: R neurons recruit both GABA and GABA-A receptors to their axon terminals in the EB.
source: R neurons recruit both GABA and GABA-A receptors to their axon terminals in the EB, and optogenetic stimulation coupled with electrophysiological recordings show that Sema-1a-dependent R axon lamination is required for preventing the spread of synaptic inhibition between adjacent EB lamina.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining and genetic labeling in Figure 6.

claim: Sema-1a-dependent R axon lamination is required for preventing the spread of synaptic inhibition between adjacent EB lamina.
source: R neurons recruit both GABA and GABA-A receptors to their axon terminals in the EB, and optogenetic stimulation coupled with electrophysiological recordings show that Sema-1a-dependent R axon lamination is required for preventing the spread of synaptic inhibition between adjacent EB lamina.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic and electrophysiological experiments in Figure 7.

claim: EB lamination is critical for local pre-synaptic inhibitory circuit organization.
source: These results provide direct evidence that EB lamination is critical for local pre-synaptic inhibitory circuit organization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: Laminated distribution of synaptic connections is an organizational feature observed in both vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems.
source: Laminated distribution of synaptic connections is an organizational feature observed in both vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems (Kolodkin and Hiesinger, 2017; Baier, 2013; Sanes and Yamagata, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms that control neuronal lamination remain to be fully elucidated.
source: However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control neuronal lamination remain to be fully elucidated, as does how laminar constraint of synaptic organization in particular brain structures contributes to function.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The insect brain is composed of myriad complex synaptic connections organized into multiple neuropil modules.
source: The insect brain, although small, is composed of myriad complex synaptic connections organized into multiple neuropil modules (Ito et al., 2014), and each module adopts distinct structural features geared toward specific functions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In Drosophila the optic lobes include heavily laminated synaptic connections.
source: For example, in Drosophila the optic lobes include heavily laminated synaptic connections (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010), while the antennal lobes include individual glomeruli where distinct olfactory sensory neurons contact to second-order neurons (Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The antennal lobes include individual glomeruli where distinct olfactory sensory neurons contact to second-order neurons.
source: For example, in Drosophila the optic lobes include heavily laminated synaptic connections (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010), while the antennal lobes include individual glomeruli where distinct olfactory sensory neurons contact to second-order neurons (Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The central complex (CX) is a highly conserved neuropil module critical for sensory integration and motor coordination functions analogous to the vertebrate basal ganglion.
source: Deep within the insect brain, a highly conserved neuropil module called the central complex (CX) is composed of several laminated structures critical for sensory integration and motor coordination functions analogous to the vertebrate basal ganglion (Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013; Strausfeld, 2012; Turner-Evans and Jayaraman, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CX is composed of four neuropil substructures: the ellipsoid body (EB), the fan-shaped body (FB), the noduli (NO) and the protocerebral bridge (PB).
source: The CX is composed of four neuropil substructures, from anterior to posterior: the ellipsoid body (EB), the fan-shaped body (FB), the noduli (NO) and the protocerebral bridge (PB) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization supported by Figure 1A schematic.

claim: In each CX substructure, neuronal processes elaborate their trajectories in precisely defined regions.
source: In each CX substructure, neuronal processes elaborate their trajectories in precisely defined regions.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

claim: CX neuronal processes form multiple layers, or laminae, from dorsal-to-ventral within the EB, FB and NO.
source: They form multiple layers, or laminae, from dorsal-to-ventral within the EB, FB and NO, and other neuronal processes form 16–18 columns, medial-to-lateral, within the EB, PB and FB.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

claim: CX neuronal processes form 16–18 columns, medial-to-lateral, within the EB, PB and FB.
source: They form multiple layers, or laminae, from dorsal-to-ventral within the EB, FB and NO, and other neuronal processes form 16–18 columns, medial-to-lateral, within the EB, PB and FB.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

claim: More than 50 different types of 'small-field' and 'large-field' neurons innervate CX substructures.
source: More than 50 different types of 'small-field' and 'large-field' neurons innervate these CX substructures (Hanesch et al., 1989; Young and Armstrong, 2010b).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Every small-field neuron innervates one or two columns and contacts one or multiple laminae in specific CX substructures.
source: Every small-field neuron innervates one or two columns and contacts one or multiple laminae in specific CX substructures.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

claim: Each large-field neuron innervates an entire single lamina across all columns in certain CX substructures.
source: On the other hand, each large-field neuron innervates an entire single lamina across all columns in certain CX substructures.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

claim: Small- and large-field neurons collaboratively form highly organized wiring patterns and are interconnected in all four CX neuropils.
source: Therefore, small- and large-field neurons collaboratively form highly organized wiring patterns and are interconnected in all four CX neuropils (Lin et al., 2013; Wolff et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2013), allowing for information flow in precisely defined patterns within the CX.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ring (R) neurons are the major large-field neurons that innervate the EB.
source: The major large-field neurons that innervate the EB are called ring (R) neurons, named for their circumferential ring-like axonal arborization patterns that form several circular laminae/rings in the anterior shell of the EB (Hanesch et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ring neurons receive pre-synaptic inputs from descending neurons of the anterior visual pathway through their dendrites located in the bulb.
source: Anatomical analyses suggest that ring neurons, through their dendrites located in the bulb (Figure 1B, arrows), receive pre-synaptic inputs from descending neurons of the anterior visual pathway (Omoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation and Figure 1B.

claim: Neuronal activity of some ring neuron dendrites correlates with light stimulation and is organized in a retinotopic fashion within the bulb.
source: Indeed, neuronal activity of some ring neuron dendrites correlates with light stimulation and is organized in a retinotopic fashion within the bulb (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Some ring neurons contribute to the circuits that influence visually evoked memory and learning.
source: Further, some ring neurons contribute to the circuits that influence visually evoked memory and learning (Wang et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2009; Neuser et al., 2008; Ofstad et al., 2011), and they are also involved in homeostatic regulation of behaviors such as hunger sensation (Park et al., 2016; Dus et al., 2013) and sleep homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ring neurons are involved in homeostatic regulation of behaviors such as hunger sensation and sleep homeostasis.
source: Further, some ring neurons contribute to the circuits that influence visually evoked memory and learning (Wang et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2009; Neuser et al., 2008; Ofstad et al., 2011), and they are also involved in homeostatic regulation of behaviors such as hunger sensation (Park et al., 2016; Dus et al., 2013) and sleep homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pb-eb-gall neurons elaborate dendrites in the EB that overlap with R neuron axons and presumably serve as their post-synaptic partners.
source: One type of small-field neuron, called 'pb-eb-gall' or 'E-PG,' elaborates dendrites in the EB that overlap with R neuron axons and presumably serves as their post-synaptic partners.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization with inference about synaptic relationships.

claim: Neuronal activity observed in pb-eb-gall neuron dendrites is tuned to the fly's head direction coordinates.
source: Neuronal activity observed in pb-eb-gall neuron dendrites is tuned to the fly's head direction coordinates (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: R2/R4m axons extend into the developing EB earlier than R3/R4d axons.
source: R2/R4m axons (red arrows) extend into the developing EB earlier than R3/R4d axons (green arrows and arrowheads), as can be observed between 16 and 24 hr APF since R2/R4m axons exhibit dense elaboration and co-localization with strong CadN staining prior to R3/R4d axons.
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 16 hr APF, many R2/R4m axons have already reached the EB.
source: At 16 hr APF, the earliest time point when it is possible to identify the EB by CadN expression, many R2/R4m axons have already reached the EB.
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments.

claim: At 16 and 20 hr APF, R3 axons were barely observed at the midline and had simple linear morphologies.
source: In contrast, CD8-GFP-labeled R3 axons were barely observed at the midline at 16 and 20 hr APF, and they appeared to have simple linear morphologies (Figure 1D, green arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: R axon projections and elaborations appear complete between 40 and 48 hr APF.
source: R axon projections and elaborations appear complete between 40 and 48 hr APF, and the overall organization of R axons after 48 hr APF shows no difference when compared to the adult brain.
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: R2/R4m, R3 and R4d axons do not overlap with one another during all the pupal stages assessed.
source: Moreover, R2/R4m, R3 and R4d axons do not overlap with one another during all the pupal stages we assessed, suggesting that they are segregated from each other soon after they arrive at the EB.
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments with inference about segregation.

claim: Pb-eb-gall neurons have columnar dendritic elaborations in the EB, extending across multiple rings over the entire EB radius.
source: In contrast to R neuron axons, small-field pb-eb-gall neurons have columnar dendritic elaborations in the EB, extending across multiple rings over the entire EB radius (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and H).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and H.

claim: Functional GFP was reconstituted between pb-eb-gall dendrites and R2/R4m (or R1/R3/R4d) axons in adult fly brains using GRASP technique.
source: When we used the GFP-reconstitution-across-synaptic-partners (GRASP) technique to determine the proximity of pb-eb-gall neuron dendrites to R neuron axons, functional GFP was reconstituted between pb-eb-gall dendrites and R2/R4m (or R1/R3/R4d) axons in adult fly brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J, green fluorescence), revealing that un-laminated pb-eb-gall dendrites closely associate with multiple types of laminated R axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from GRASP experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: At 16–24 hr APF, pb-eb-gall dendrites adopt a crescent shape within the EB.
source: At 16–24 hr APF, pb-eb-gall dendrites adopt a crescent shape within the EB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L, blue dashed lines).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: At 16–24 hr APF, pb-eb-gall dendrites overlap with R2/R4m axons but do not overlap with R3/R4d axons.
source: They overlap with R2/R4m axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K, red arrows) but do not overlap with R3/R4d axons at these stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L, red arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: At 48 hr APF, pb-eb-gall dendrites extend ventrally to form a complete circle and expand inwardly to occupy the entire radius of the EB.
source: At later pupal stages, pb-eb-gall dendrites extend ventrally to form a complete circle and also expand inwardly such that pb-eb-gall dendrites occupy the entire radius of the EB and overlap with both R2/R4m and R3/R4d axons, as can be appreciated at 48 hr APF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L, bottom panels).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: The development of pb-eb-gall dendrites and R axons is highly correlated during the EB formation.
source: These data suggest that the development of pb-eb-gall dendrites and R axons is highly correlated during the EB formation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference from the developmental imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The select association between pb-eb-gall dendrites and R2/R4m axons at early pupal developmental stages suggests an instructive role for pb-eb-gall neurons with respect to R neuron axon targeting and lamina formation.
source: Further, the select association between pb-eb-gall dendrites and R2/R4m axons at early pupal developmental stages suggests an instructive role for pb-eb-gall neurons with respect to R neuron axon targeting and lamina formation.
evidence: This is an inference from the developmental imaging data.

claim: Ablation of pb-eb-gall neurons led to pronounced R2/R4m axon patterning defects in the EB.
source: DTI expression by R19G02-GAL4 from wL3 stages ablated most pb-eb-gall neurons (arrowheads) and led to pronounced R2/R4m axon patterning defects in the EB (red oval) (n = 14 animals).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ablation of pb-eb-gall neurons resulted in gross changes in R3/R4d axon patterning in the EB.
source: Similar lamination defects were observed in R3/R4d axons, labeled by R70B04-lexA-driving mtdT, when pb-eb-gall neurons were ablated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, red circle and oval).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ablation of pb-eb-no neurons did not cause apparent defects to the R2/R4m ring morphologies.
source: However, ablation of another type of small-field neuron called 'pb-eb-no' or 'P-EN' (Wolff et al., 2015; Omoto et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017) that also elaborates processes in the EB during early pupal stages, using the R83H12-GAL4 driver, did not cause apparent defects to the R2/R4m ring morphologies (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments.

claim: Pb-eb-gall neurons are selectively required for instructing R neuron axon patterning during EB development.
source: These results show that pb-eb-gall neurons are selectively required for instructing R neuron axon patterning during EB development.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: Ablation of R2/R4m neurons led to a 29% reduction in pb-eb-gall dendrite areas at 48 hr ATS.
source: Upon the loss of a substantial fraction of R2/R4m neurons, the EB was reduced in size and pb-eb-gall dendrite areas were 29% smaller than in controls 48 hr ATS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, green circles; quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The areas occupied by pb-eb-gall axon terminals in the gall remained unchanged following R2/R4m ablation.
source: In contrast, the areas occupied by pb-eb-gall axon terminals in the gall remained unchanged in control and in R2/R4m ablation animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, blue arrow and arrowhead; quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: R2/R4m axons are required locally for pb-eb-gall dendrite growth in the EB.
source: These observations show that R2/R4m axons are required locally for pb-eb-gall dendrite growth in the EB.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: When R2/R4m neurons were ablated, R3 axon arbors occupied a larger area (26.6% increase) at 48 hr ATS.
source: When R2/R4m neurons were ablated, R3 axon arbors occupied a larger area (26.6% increase) at 48 hr ATS; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, green ovals; quantification in Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments shown in Figure 2C, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: R2/R4m ring neurons influence the size of R3 ring neuron axon arborizations.
source: Therefore, R2/R4m ring neurons influence the size of R3 ring neuron axon arborizations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: Loss of >60% of R1/R3/R4d neurons had no observable effects on EB morphology or R2/R4m axon expansion.
source: In contrast to what we observed following ablation of R2/R4m neurons, loss of >60% of GFP-labeled R1/R3/R4d neurons (with the remaining R1/R3/R4d neurons exhibiting >10 fold reduction in GFP expression) had no observable effects on EB morphology or R2/R4m axon expansion (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from ablation experiments.

claim: Pb-eb-gall dendrites and axons from different R neuron types play distinct roles in EB neuronal process development.
source: These neuron ablation experiments suggest that pb-eb-gall dendrites and axons from different R neuron types play distinct roles in EB neuronal process development.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: The pb-eb-gall neurons are critical for the EB morphogenesis and axon patterning of all R types examined.
source: The pb-eb-gall neurons are critical for the EB morphogenesis and axon patterning of all R types we examined.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: Outer R2/R4m axons constrain inner R3 axon arbor expansion.
source: In addition, outer R2/R4m axons constrain inner R3 axon arbor expansion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claim: Sema-1a is expressed in the EB during pupal stages.
source: Using antibodies against the transmembrane semaphorin Sema-1a (Yu et al., 1998) and its receptor plexin A (PlexA) (Sweeney et al., 2007), we detected expression of both proteins in the central complex during early pupal stages (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B). Both proteins are detected in the EB during pupal stages (Figure 3A and B, arrowheads), and Sema-1a is also found in the bulb (Figure 3A, arrows), where R neuron dendrites project.
evidence: This is a finding from antibody staining shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PlexA is expressed in the EB during pupal stages.
source: Using antibodies against the transmembrane semaphorin Sema-1a (Yu et al., 1998) and its receptor plexin A (PlexA) (Sweeney et al., 2007), we detected expression of both proteins in the central complex during early pupal stages (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B). Both proteins are detected in the EB during pupal stages (Figure 3A and B, arrowheads), and Sema-1a is also found in the bulb (Figure 3A, arrows), where R neuron dendrites project.
evidence: This is a finding from antibody staining shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sema-1a is found in the bulb where R neuron dendrites project.
source: Both proteins are detected in the EB during pupal stages (Figure 3A and B, arrowheads), and Sema-1a is also found in the bulb (Figure 3A, arrows), where R neuron dendrites project.
evidence: This is a finding from antibody staining shown in Figure 3A.

claim: V5-tagged Sema-1a is specifically enriched in R neuron axonal terminals within the EB at 24 hr APF and at 48 hr APF.
source: High-magnification images reveal that V5-tagged Sema-1a is specifically enriched in R neuron axonal terminals within the EB at 24 hr APF (E) and at 48 hr APF, unlike CD2-GFP, which is uniformly localized in both R neuron soma and axons (F).
evidence: This is a finding from conditional tagging experiments shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Sema-1a-V5 is found in R neuron dendritic terminals in the bulb at 48 hr APF.
source: Sema-1a-V5 exhibits strong expression throughout the EB, and it is also found in R neuron dendritic terminals in the bulb at 48 hr APF.
evidence: This is a finding from conditional tagging experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Sema-1a is expressed in most R neurons with the exception of a small subset of R2/R4m cells.
source: Indeed, dual labeling experiments using different GAL4 drivers (R11F03-GAL4 for R1-R4; R15F02-GAL4 for R1/R3/R4d; EB-GAL4 for R2/R4m) confirmed that Sema-1a is expressed in most R neurons (Figure 3I and J, red) with the exception of a small subset of R2/R4m cells that are labeled only by GFP but not mCherry (Figure 3J, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from conditional tagging experiments shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Knocking down Sema-1a in R2/R4m neurons resulted in a 32.1% and 27.1% increase in the areas including R2/R4m synaptic labeling for two different Sema-1a-RNAi lines.
source: By measuring the areas covered by Syt-GFP immunostaining, we found that the areas including R2/R4m synaptic labeling were increased by 32.1% and 27.1% in two different Sema-1a-RNAi lines, and by 19.3% and 22.8% in two different PlexA-RNAi lines, compared to controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Knocking down PlexA in R2/R4m neurons resulted in a 19.3% and 22.8% increase in the areas including R2/R4m synaptic labeling for two different PlexA-RNAi lines.
source: By measuring the areas covered by Syt-GFP immunostaining, we found that the areas including R2/R4m synaptic labeling were increased by 32.1% and 27.1% in two different Sema-1a-RNAi lines, and by 19.3% and 22.8% in two different PlexA-RNAi lines, compared to controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Both Sema-1a and PlexA are required for constraining R2/4m axon arbor growth in an EB layer-autonomous manner.
source: These data reveal that both Sema-1a and PlexA are required for constraining R2/4m axon arbor growth in what appears to be an EB layer-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi experiments.

claim: In Sema-1a-/- clones containing multiple R2 and R4m neurons, Syt-HA-labeled axon terminals expanded inwardly within the EB.
source: In a Sema-1a-/- clone containing multiple R2 and R4m cells, Syt-HA-labeled axon terminals expanded inwardly within the EB, recapitulating the Sema-1a-RNAi phenotype in panel A.
evidence: This is a finding from MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Outer EB lamination phenotype was only observed in Sema-1a-/- clones consisting of R4m neurons, but not in clones composed of only R2 cells.
source: Interestingly, this outer EB lamination phenotype was only observed in Sema-1a-/- clones consisting of R4m neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but not in clones composed of only R2 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: R2/R4m axon lamination defects in Sema-1a LOF experiments are largely due to lack of Sema-1a in R4m neurons.
source: These results show that R2/R4m axon lamination defects in Sema-1a LOF experiments are largely due to lack of Sema-1a in R4m neurons, underscoring the select interactions among ring neurons that are required to generate EB laminar organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the MARCM experiments.

claim: Single Sema-1a-/- R4m neurons had aberrant axon arbor morphology.
source: Indeed, compared to control R4m neurons (Figure 4Di), single Sema-1a-/- R4m neurons had aberrant axon arbor morphology (Figure 4Dii).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Some synaptic boutons in Sema-1a-/- R4m neurons were localized to more central EB regions.
source: Further, some synaptic boutons, identified by both GFP-labeled varicosities and Syt-HA labeling (Figure 4Dii, small panels, arrowheads), were localized to more central EB regions (Figure 4Dii, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expression of full-length Sema-1a, but not Sema-1aEcTM, in Sema-1a-/- R4m cells rescued R4m axon arbor phenotypes.
source: Expression of Sema-1a, but not Sema-1aEcTM, in Sema-1a-/- R4m cells rescued R4m axon arbor phenotypes (Figure 4Diii and 4Div).
evidence: This is a finding from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The smallest distances between R4m boutons and the EB center were significantly decreased in Sema-1a-/- and in Sema-1aEcTM rescue neurons compared to control R neurons.
source: The smallest distances, which indicate how close R4m boutons are to the EB center, were significantly decreased in Sema-1a-/- (11.85 ± 2.36 μm, n = 16 singe-cell clones [SSCs]) and in Sema-1aEcTM rescue (9.34 ± 1.64 μm, n = 10 SSCs) neurons but showed no difference compared to control R neurons (15.95 ± 1.93 μm, n = 12 SSCs) or Sema-1a rescue R neurons (14.62 ± 1.64 μm, n = 9 SSCs) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of single-cell MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A significantly larger fraction of R4m boutons was found in the central EB region in both Sema-1a-/- (4.66%) and Sema-1aEcTM rescue (10.52%) compared to the control group (0.62%).
source: A significantly larger fraction of R4m boutons was found in the central EB region in both Sema-1a-/- (4.66%, n = 16 SSCs) and Sema-1aEcTM rescue (10.52%, n = 10 SSCs) compared to the control group (0.62%, n = 12 SSCs).
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of single-cell MARCM experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Full length Sema-1a, but not truncated Sema-1a lacking its cytoplasmic domain, is required cell-autonomously to regulate R4m axon branch growth, lamination and synapse distribution within the EB.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that full length Sema-1a, but not truncated Sema-1a lacking its cytoplasmic domain, is required cell-autonomously to regulate R4m axon branch growth, lamination and synapse distribution within the EB.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the MARCM and rescue experiments.

claim: Sema-1a functions are likely mediated through a Sema-1a 'reverse signaling' pathway in which the Sema-1a protein functions as a receptor in R4m neurons and PlexA protein servers as its ligand in other EB neurons.
source: Therefore, these functions are likely mediated through a Sema-1a 'reverse signaling' pathway in which the Sema-1a protein functions as a receptor in R4m neurons and PlexA protein servers as its ligand in other EB neurons (Battistini and Tamagnone, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: Down-regulation of Sema-1a using R40G10-GAL4 resulted in the EB partially losing its circular shape.
source: In Sema-1a-RNAi–expressing animals, the EB partially lost its circular shape.
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Down-regulation of PlexA using R40G10-GAL4 resulted in the EB remaining completely open and R4m axons expanding their axon projections to cover most EB regions.
source: More severe phenotypes were observed in PlexA-RNAi expressing animals. In many R40G10>PlexA-RNAi animals, the EB remained completely open and R4m axons expanded their axon projections to cover most EB regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Aiii and Avi).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PlexA in R1–3, and most likely in R2 alone, plays an important role in regulating R4m axon lamination formation through Sema-1a reverse signaling pathway.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that PlexA in R1–3, and most likely in R2 alone since knocking down PlexA in R1/R3 with multiple drivers did not generate similar defects (data not shown), plays an important role in regulating R4m axon lamination formation through Sema-1a reverse signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi experiments with inference.

claim: In Sema-1a-RNAi or PlexA-RNAi–expressing fly lines, R3 axon arbors expand outward within the EB.
source: However, in either R2/R4m Sema-1a-RNAi or PlexA-RNAi–expressing fly lines, R3 axon arbors expand outward within the EB (Figure 5Av and 5Avi), and this is accompanied by inward expansion of R2/R4m axons (Figure 5Aii and 5Aiii).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Following normalization to controls, the area occupied by R3 axon arbors increased 48.3 ± 15.6% and 42.8 ± 12.4% for the two independent Sema-1a-RNAi lines.
source: Following normalization to controls (n = 8 animals), the area occupied by R3 axon arbors increased 48.3 ± 15.6% (n = 8 brains) and 42.8 ± 12.4% (n = 7 brains) for the two independent Sema-1a-RNAi lines, and 34.8 ± 28.7% (n = 8 brains) and 50.4 ± 32.6% (n = 8 brains) for the two independent PlexA-RNAi lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Following normalization to controls, the area occupied by R3 axon arbors increased 34.8 ± 28.7% and 50.4 ± 32.6% for the two independent PlexA-RNAi lines.
source: Following normalization to controls (n = 8 animals), the area occupied by R3 axon arbors increased 48.3 ± 15.6% (n = 8 brains) and 42.8 ± 12.4% (n = 7 brains) for the two independent Sema-1a-RNAi lines, and 34.8 ± 28.7% (n = 8 brains) and 50.4 ± 32.6% (n = 8 brains) for the two independent PlexA-RNAi lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sema-1a/PlexA-dependent R2/R4m axon patterning is required to control R3 axon expansion through a local repellent signal.
source: Taken together, these results support the idea that Sema-1a/PlexA-dependent R2/R4m axon patterning is required to control R3 axon expansion through a local repellent signal, thereby regulating R axon lamination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Knocking down Sema-1a or PlexA in R3 neurons did not change the size or morphology of the R3 rings.
source: First, we found that knocking down Sema-1a or PlexA in R3 neurons did not change the size or morphology of the R3 rings (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Single R3 axon ring diameters are not different between control and Sema-1a-/- R3 neurons.
source: Second, MARCM experiments show that single R3 axon ring diameters are not different between control and Sema-1a-/- R3 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F; 'Diameter' quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from MARCM experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: In Sema-1a-/- single R3 MARCM clones, many R3 neurons elaborate axon branches that grow more posteriorly within the EB, and for some R3 neurons out of the EB and into the posterior FB.
source: However, in Sema-1a-/- single R3 MARCM clones, many R3 neurons elaborate axon branches that grow more posteriorly within the EB, and for some R3 neurons (6 out of 21 cells) out of the EB and into the posterior FB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F; quantification of 'R3 Thickness' in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from MARCM experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F and G.

claim: Sema-1a controls longer range R axon extension to secure the overall separation of neighboring brain structures.
source: This suggests that Sema-1a controls longer range R axon extension to secure the overall separation of neighboring brain structures.
evidence: This is an inference from the MARCM experiments.

claim: It is unlikely PlexA or Sema-1a act in R3 as receptors for R2/R4m Sema-1a or PlexA to directly regulate R3 axon growth.
source: Together, these results show that it is unlikely PlexA or Sema-1a act in R3 as receptors for R2/R4m Sema-1a or PlexA to directly regulate R3 axon growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi and MARCM experiments.

claim: R2/R4m axons use other molecules to constrain R3 axons and refine axon patterning and lamination during pupal development.
source: Although we find that Sema-1a and PlexA function in R2/R4m neurons to organize axon lamination, our data suggest that R2/R4m axons use other molecules to constrain R3 axons and refine axon patterning and lamination during pupal development.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined experimental results.

claim: Pb-eb-gall dendrites appeared normal when R2/R4m axons expanded their elaboration within the EB in either Sema-1a-RNAi or PlexA-RNAi–expressing animals.
source: The pb-eb-gall dendrites appeared normal when R2/R4m axons expanded their elaboration within the EB in either Sema-1a-RNAi or PlexA-RNAi–expressing animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Aiv-vi).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Reconstituted GFP was detected in the EB in both control and UAS-Sema-1a-RNAi-expressing animals using syb:GRASP technique.
source: Reconstituted GFP (rcGFP) was detected in the EB in both control and UAS-Sema-1a-RNAi-expressing animals, even though different GFP fluorescence patterns were observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from syb:GRASP experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: R axon lamination defects do not affect pb-eb-gall dendrite elaboration or synaptogenesis between R axons and pb-eb-gall dendrites.
source: These data suggest that R axon lamination defects do not affect pb-eb-gall dendrite elaboration or synaptogenesis between R axons and pb-eb-gall dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi and GRASP experiments.

claim: Knocking down Sema-1a or PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons partially or completely re-directed their axon projections from the gall to a region close to the EB.
source: Knocking down Sema-1a or PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons partially or completely re-directed their axon projections from the gall (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Ci-iii and Di-iii, arrows) to a region close to the EB (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Ci-iii and Di-iii, arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Loss of Sema-1a or PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons did not affect pb-eb-gall dendrite elaboration or R2/4 m and R3/R4d axon lamination.
source: However, loss of Sema-1a or PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons did not affect pb-eb-gall dendrite elaboration or R2/4 m and R3/R4d axon lamination (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Civ-vi and Div-vi), suggesting that Sema-1a and PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons are not required for pb-eb-gall dendrite or R axon development in the EB.
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Sema-1a and PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons are not required for pb-eb-gall dendrite or R axon development in the EB.
source: However, loss of Sema-1a or PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons did not affect pb-eb-gall dendrite elaboration or R2/4 m and R3/R4d axon lamination (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Civ-vi and Div-vi), suggesting that Sema-1a and PlexA in pb-eb-gall neurons are not required for pb-eb-gall dendrite or R axon development in the EB.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Abundant protein expression of GABA and RDL has been observed in the EB and appears to be closely associated with R neuron axons.
source: Abundant protein expression of gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) and RDL (a GABA-A receptor subunit) has been observed in the EB and appears to be closely associated with R neuron axons (Kahsai et al., 2012; Martín-Peña et al., 2014; Enell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A group of R2/R4m neurons are GABAergic and thermogenetic activation of these neurons impairs medium-term olfactory memory.
source: However, the sources of GABA and RDL and their functions in the EB are largely unknown, although a group of R2/R4m neurons are known to be GABAergic and thermogenetic activation of these neurons impairs medium-term olfactory memory (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Fluorescent reporters driven by Gad1MI-QF2 and RdlMI-GAL4 were both expressed in a large number of R neurons.
source: We found that fluorescent reporters driven by Gad1MI-QF2 and RdlMI-GAL4 (Diao et al., 2015) were both expressed in a large number of R neurons, displaying characteristic axon trajectories into the bulb and EB (Figure 6A and D, arrowheads and arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from genetic labeling experiments shown in Figure 6A and D.

claim: Expression of UAS-Gad1-RNAi in R2/R4m neurons decreased GABA immunoreactivity in the peripheral EB.
source: Expression of either UAS-Gad1-RNAi or UAS-Rdl-RNAi in R2/R4m neurons using R32H08-GAL4 decreased GABA and RDL immunoreactivity, respectively, in the peripheral EB, the location where R2/R4m axons project (Figure 6B arrowhead; Figure 6E, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of UAS-Rdl-RNAi in R2/R4m neurons decreased RDL immunoreactivity in the peripheral EB.
source: Expression of either UAS-Gad1-RNAi or UAS-Rdl-RNAi in R2/R4m neurons using R32H08-GAL4 decreased GABA and RDL immunoreactivity, respectively, in the peripheral EB, the location where R2/R4m axons project (Figure 6B arrowhead; Figure 6E, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression levels of GABA and RDL were reduced in central EB regions when R3 Gal4 drivers were used to express corresponding RNAi transgenes.
source: Expression levels of GABA and RDL were also reduced in central EB regions when R3 Gal4 drivers were used to express these corresponding RNAi transgenes (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAi experiments.

claim: Many fewer cholinergic, glutamatergic or dopaminergic inputs were observed in the EB, and most of these were preferentially localized to posterior EB regions.
source: Many fewer cholinergic, glutamatergic or dopaminergic inputs were observed in the EB, and most of these were preferentially localized to posterior EB regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from antibody staining and genetic labeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple types of R neurons are GABAergic and recruit GABA-A receptors to their axon terminals in the EB.
source: Taken together, these results show that multiple types of R neurons are GABAergic and also that they recruit GABA-A receptors to their axon terminals in the EB, raising the question of whether R axon lamination influences EB inhibitory synaptic properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic labeling and RNAi experiments.

claim: Following loss of pb-eb-gall neurons, R2/R4m and R3/R4d axons likely intermingle with one another in DTI-expressing animals.
source: Both R2/R4m and R3/R4d axons appear to occupy the entire EB and therefore likely intermingle with one another in DTI-expressing animals.
evidence: This is an inference from the ablation experiments.

claim: LED stimulation of R3 neurons had little effect on evoking APs in R2/R4m neurons in control animals.
source: More importantly, LED stimulation of R3 neurons had little effect on evoking APs in R2/R4m neurons in these control animals (Figure 7C and D, red vs blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic and electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The slopes of the f-I curves were no different when the LED light was off or on in control brains (0.142 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.125 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.391).
source: The slopes of the f-I curves were no different when the LED light was off or on in control brains (0.142 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.125 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.391) (Figure 7E), showing that the excitability of R2/R4m neurons is not coupled to R3 activation when R2/R4m and R3 axons are physically separated into two adjacent laminae in WT animals.
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The excitability of R2/R4m neurons is not coupled to R3 activation when R2/R4m and R3 axons are physically separated into two adjacent laminae in WT animals.
source: The slopes of the f-I curves were no different when the LED light was off or on in control brains (0.142 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.125 ± 0.032 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.391) (Figure 7E), showing that the excitability of R2/R4m neurons is not coupled to R3 activation when R2/R4m and R3 axons are physically separated into two adjacent laminae in WT animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Following R3 neuron activation (LED on) in Sema-1a-RNAi animals, R2/R4m neurons generated many fewer APs when evoked with the same depolarization currents above the current threshold.
source: However, following R3 neuron activation (LED on) in these Sema-1a-RNAi animals, R2/R4m neurons generated many fewer APs when evoked with the same depolarization currents above the current threshold (Figure 7F and G, red vs blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic and electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: The slopes of f-I curves were significantly decreased in Sema-1a-RNAi expressing animals when the LED light was on (0.208 ± 0.074 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.05 ± 0.019 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.023).
source: In contrast to controls, the slopes of f-I curves were significantly decreased in Sema-1a-RNAi expressing animals when the LED light was on (0.208 ± 0.074 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.05 ± 0.019 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.023) (Figure 7H), showing that it is more difficult to evoke APs in R2/R4m neurons when light-activated R3 axons are intermingled with R2/R4m axons in Sema-1a-RNAi brains.
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7H.

claim: It is more difficult to evoke APs in R2/R4m neurons when light-activated R3 axons are intermingled with R2/R4m axons in Sema-1a-RNAi brains.
source: In contrast to controls, the slopes of f-I curves were significantly decreased in Sema-1a-RNAi expressing animals when the LED light was on (0.208 ± 0.074 Hz/pA for LED-off vs 0.05 ± 0.019 Hz/pA for LED-on, p=0.023) (Figure 7H), showing that it is more difficult to evoke APs in R2/R4m neurons when light-activated R3 axons are intermingled with R2/R4m axons in Sema-1a-RNAi brains.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: LED stimulation of R3 resulted in no change of Vm or Rin in R2/R4m neurons in control animals.
source: Consistently, LED stimulation of R3 resulted in no change of Vm (−56.45 ± 5.16 mV for LED-off vs −57.14 ± 6.33 mV for LED-on, p=0.546) or Rin (1.105 ± 0.157 GOhm for LED-off vs 1.120 ± 0.148 GOhm for LED-on, p=0.822) in R2/R4m neurons in control animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: In Sema-1a-RNAi-expressing animals, R3 activation significantly hyperpolarized the Vm (−58.60 ± 1.20 mV for LED-off vs −63.26 ± 2.69 mV for LED-on, p=0.031) and decreased the Rin of R2/R4m neurons (1.001 ± 0.299 GOhm for LED-off vs 0.803 ± 0.365 GOhm for LED-on, p=0.014).
source: However, in Sema-1a-RNAi-expressing animals, R3 activation significantly hyperpolarized the Vm (−58.60 ± 1.20 mV for LED-off vs −63.26 ± 2.69 mV for LED-on, p=0.031) and decreased the Rin of R2/R4m neurons (1.001 ± 0.299 GOhm for LED-off vs 0.803 ± 0.365 GOhm for LED-on, p=0.014) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: R3 activation acutely altered the electrophysiological properties of R2/R4m cell membranes when Sema-1a-mediated axon lamination was disrupted.
source: These results indicate that R3 activation acutely altered the electrophysiological properties of R2/R4m cell membranes when Sema-1a-mediated axon lamination was disrupted.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: When Sema-1a-mediated R axon lamination is disrupted, R3 and R2/R4m axons exhibit ectopic contacts, aberrantly coupling their activity through ectopic inhibitory synapses.
source: Taken together, these data support the idea that when Sema-1a-mediated R axon lamination is disrupted, R3 and R2/R4m axons exhibit ectopic contacts, aberrantly coupling their activity through ectopic inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined anatomical and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Laminar organization of R axons plays an important role in specifying inhibitory synapse formation between different types of R axons in the EB.
source: Therefore, laminar organization of R axons plays an important role in specifying inhibitory synapse formation between different types of R axons in the EB.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined anatomical and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: All ring neurons share a common progenitor lineage and follow similar trajectories as their axons approach the brain midline.
source: All ring neurons share a common progenitor lineage and follow similar trajectories as their axons approach the brain midline (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple R neuron types have been identified based on their different axonal arbor morphologies in the EB and also by analysis of different enhancer trap lines.
source: Multiple R neuron types have been identified based on their different axonal arbor morphologies in the EB and also by analysis of different enhancer trap lines that uniquely express the transcriptional activator GAL4 in R neuron types (Hanesch et al., 1989; Renn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: N-Cadherin (CadN) is a cell adhesion molecule widely expressed in the developing nervous system that consolidates target selection between pre- and post-synaptic neurons.
source: N-Cadherin (CadN) is a cell adhesion molecule widely expressed in the developing nervous system that consolidates target selection between pre- and post-synaptic neurons (Iwai et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CadN immunostaining shows that the ellipsoid body forms during early pupal stages.
source: CadN immunostaining shows that the ellipsoid body forms during early pupal stages (Young and Armstrong, 2010a).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The EB emerges at around 16 hr after pupae formation (APF) with an open crescent shape.
source: Our results confirm that the EB emerges at around 16 hr (16 hr) after pupae formation (APF) with an open crescent shape that in later developmental stages closes toward the ventral side; the complete circular EB morphology is apparent between 40 and 48 hr APF (Figure 1D, white dashed lines in panels on right; Figure 1E, light blue schematics).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The complete circular EB morphology is apparent between 40 and 48 hr APF.
source: Our results confirm that the EB emerges at around 16 hr (16 hr) after pupae formation (APF) with an open crescent shape that in later developmental stages closes toward the ventral side; the complete circular EB morphology is apparent between 40 and 48 hr APF (Figure 1D, white dashed lines in panels on right; Figure 1E, light blue schematics).
evidence: This is a finding from developmental imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D and E.
